judgments.yea_description: Voted for Legislative Bill 229, which takes app-based gig workers out of Nebraska's unemployment system. The Employment Security Law funds and pays unemployment benefits. The act adds these workers to the list of people whose work does not count as employment under it. It covers a person who signs up through a company's app to be matched with customers. The person must be paid for that work and must not work at a site the company runs. Four things have to be true for the exclusion to apply. The worker and the company must agree in writing that the worker is an independent contractor. The company must not set the hours the worker has to be free. It must not stop the worker taking other work, except while they are on its jobs. And it must not be able to end the contract because the worker turned a job down. The exclusion does not apply where federal law requires the work to be covered. The Nebraska Legislature passed it 33-15, and it became law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for Legislative Bill 241, which shields companies from class action lawsuits over data breaches. A business cannot be held liable in a class action over a cybersecurity event. The one exception is where the business was willfully, wantonly or grossly negligent. Ordinary carelessness is no longer enough. A cybersecurity event means someone gets into a computer system without permission. It also covers disrupting or misusing that system, or the private data kept on it. Private data here means information that can identify a person. It has to be paired with a Social Security number, a license or state ID number, a bank or card number, a password or access code, or a biometric record. The shield covers businesses run for profit and not for profit alike. Religious and charitable groups are covered too. The Nebraska Legislature passed it 36-10, and it became law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for Legislative Bill 9, which closes a gap in the state's nicotine rules. Nebraska's rules on vapes and other nicotine products covered products that contain nicotine. Makers had begun using lab-made stand-ins that act like nicotine but are not nicotine. That put those products outside the rules. The act adds the term nicotine analogue and applies the same rules to it. A nicotine analogue is a substance built much like nicotine. It also covers one whose effect on the nervous system is much like nicotine's, or stronger. The act brings these products under the tobacco tax law as well. It updates how that law is enforced, including seizing product on which no tax was paid. The Nebraska Legislature passed it 34-10, and it became law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for Legislative Bill 48, which sets up a center to keep young people out of the justice system. The Department of Health and Human Services must run a five-year pilot program. It runs in cities of the metropolitan class, which in Nebraska means Omaha. The center must be open twenty-four hours a day, every day. It has to be built with local community groups. It also has to be built with advisers who speak for young people and families the juvenile justice system has touched. The center offers support, assessment and help to young people in that system. It serves those at risk of entering it too. Its stated aim is to deal with what lies behind youth offending. That means family problems, mental health, substance abuse and trouble at school. The program ends five years after the act takes effect. The Nebraska Legislature passed it 27-21, and it became law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for Legislative Bill 275, which protects the Social Security money of children in state care. The state must check every child in its charge for Social Security within sixty days. It must apply for the benefits, and appeal a denial where that is in the child's interest. It must tell the child, in words suited to their age, about each decision within ten days. It must tell the child's lawyer and parents too. It must also tell them that an adult the child knows can ask to receive the money instead. When the state does receive the money, it must hold it in a separate trust account for that child. It must keep the money below the federal limits that would cost the child other benefits. It must account for every dollar to the juvenile court at each review hearing. The state may still use some of the money to repay itself for the cost of the child's care. But the act sets a share it may not touch. That share is twenty percent at age fourteen and thirty percent at sixteen. It is forty percent at seventeen and half at eighteen. A child of fourteen or older must be asked every six months what they need. They may also ask the juvenile court to have the money used a different way. The Nebraska Legislature passed it 29-19, and it became law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for Legislative Bill 203, which limits what a local health department can order on its own. A community-wide directed health measure now needs written approval from elected officials before the health director may issue it. For most departments that means a majority of the county board. For a city-county department it means a majority of the city council. In a city-county department serving a county of more than 200,000 people, it means the elected county board and city council members who sit on its board of health. The order then goes to the board of health to be ratified at a meeting. It expires after seven days unless it is approved again. The act defines a community-wide measure as a public health action covering everyone in the department's area when there is no known epidemiological link. An epidemiological link means someone may have been exposed to a disease in a way that disease is known to spread. So an order aimed at people tied to a known chain of infection is untouched. The Nebraska Legislature passed it 35-12, and it became law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for Legislative Bill 397, which ends the workplace safety committee rule for private employers. Since 1994 every employer covered by the workers' compensation law had to have a safety committee. The committee wrote and kept up a plan for preventing injuries at that workplace. The act keeps that duty for public employers and drops it for private ones. It also removes going without a committee as a reason an insurer may cancel a policy, or refuse to renew one. The state program that advised employers on workplace safety is repealed. Its fund is closed, and the money left in it goes to the state's general fund. The Nebraska Legislature passed it 35-13, and it became law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for Legislative Bill 795, which raises the penalties for dealing in fentanyl and bans a new synthetic drug. The act adds bromazolam, a lab-made sedative, to Schedule I, the list of drugs Nebraska treats as having no accepted medical use. It also sets penalties for handling fentanyl that rise with the amount. One hundred forty grams or more is a Class IB felony. At least twenty-eight grams but less than one hundred forty is a Class IC felony. At least ten grams but less than twenty-eight is a Class ID felony. The act corrects the spelling of several drug names in the same list. The Nebraska Legislature passed it 32-14, and it became law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for Legislative Bill 1067, which raises a tax on property sales to pay for workforce housing. Nebraska charges a documentary stamp tax when the deed to a property changes hands. The act raises it by one dollar for each thousand dollars of value. The rate goes from two dollars and thirty-two cents to three dollars and thirty-two cents. It returns to the old rate for sales on or after January 1, 2032. Fifty cents of the extra dollar goes to the Rural Workforce Housing Investment Fund. The other fifty cents goes to the Middle Income Workforce Housing Investment Fund. The act also stops money being moved out of the Affordable Housing Trust Fund from July 1, 2027. What that fund collects stays in it. The Nebraska Legislature passed it 36-13, and it became law.
